chapter_theme: In the Thuyilezhuppiya Kaathai the goddess Manimekala, having hidden the girl on Manipallavam, warns the prince that a swerving sceptre ruins planets, rain and life, and wakes Sudhamathi with the news that a ripened cause has set Manimekalai on the Buddha's path; through a sleeping city Sudhamathi goes to the hall of the Chakravala kottam, where the painted pillar image reveals the two women's former births, and at dawn she tells Madhavi, who sits stricken at her daughter's absence.

cast.role: the sea goddess for whom Manimekalai was named
the Chola king's son, who desires Manimekalai
Manimekalai's companion; Virai in a former birth
Manimekalai's father, who named her after the sea goddess
the painted image on the pillar of the Chakravala kottam's hall, which speaks

manimekalai:7:1-14.reading: Having left Manimekalai on Manipallavam, the goddess Manimekala appears before the sleepless prince Udayakumaran, who expects to have the girl in his hands by morning, and warns him that if the sceptre swerves the planets swerve, rain fails and no life is left, so that the king can no longer be called the life of all beings; he must drop the wrongful intent he has set on one who has taken up tapas.
manimekalai:7:1-14.nuance: The goddess treats a prince's desire for a renouncer as a swerving of the sceptre itself, though he is only the heir and has judged no case; the fault is private desire, and the stakes she names are cosmic. Lines 11-12 can be read either as all beings calling the king their life or as all beings being the king's own life; on either reading the title lapses because the beings it rests on are gone.
manimekalai:7:1-14.event: The goddess Manimekala appears to the sleepless prince Udayakumaran and warns him to give up his designs on Manimekalai.

claims.claim: when the ruler's sceptre swerves, the planets leave their course, rain fails and living beings perish
a king keeps the standing of being the life of all beings only while his rule holds them alive
to set desire on a woman who has taken up tapas is a wrongful intent a ruler must give up

manimekalai:7:1-14.unit_note: The core unit 1-24 is split at line 14, where the speech to the prince closes with ஒழிக' என்று and the goddess turns to Sudhamathi.

manimekalai:7:15-25.reading: The goddess then enters the Uvavanam, wakes Sudhamathi, tells her not to fear because she is Manimekala come to see the city's Indra festival, and says that since the cause for the young girl to enter the great sage's path of dharma has ripened, she has carried her by magic to Manipallavam, from where, having come to know her former birth, the girl will appear near the city in seven days.
manimekalai:7:15-25.nuance: The goddess does not say she chose to act: she acts because a cause (ஏது) has ripened, so the rescue is the working-out of a condition, not a divine decision. Her self-announcement வந்தேன் அஞ்சல் மணிமேகலை யான் is word for word the formula she spoke to Kovalan's shipwrecked ancestor in the Silappathikaram (15, line 33).
manimekalai:7:15-25.event: The goddess wakes Sudhamathi in the Uvavanam and tells her she has carried Manimekalai to Manipallavam, from where the girl will return in seven days knowing her former birth.

claims.claim: one enters the Buddha's path of dharma when the cause for it has ripened

manimekalai:7:15-25.unit_note: Starts at line 15, where the goddess leaves the prince for the grove; the core boundary after line 24 is moved to line 25, which closes the sentence begun at 23 (வந்து தோன்றும் மடக்கொடி நல்லாள்).

manimekalai:7:26-39.reading: The goddess adds that the girl, even if she enters the city in a changed form, will not hide herself from Sudhamathi, that many things are caused to happen here on the day she comes, and bids her tell Madhavi of this visit, for Madhavi will know her: on the night Kovalan, saying there is a goddess in the sea, gave the child her name, she told Madhavi in a dream as vivid as waking that she had borne a great creeper of tapas who would cut the cruel harm and leave Kama helpless.
manimekalai:7:26-39.nuance: The naming that the Silappathikaram tells as gratitude for a rescue at sea is given here a second, hidden meaning: the same night the goddess marked the infant for tapas. The forecast that she will come in another form (ஒளித்து உரு எய்தினும்) points ahead to her disguise as Kayasandigai.
manimekalai:7:26-39.event: The goddess bids Sudhamathi tell Madhavi of her visit, recalling the dream she gave Madhavi on the night Kovalan named the child Manimekalai.
manimekalai:7:26-39.unit_note: Starts at line 26 (the core unit began at 25, which ends the preceding sentence) and ends at line 39, where the goddess's speech closes with உரை' என்று, instead of at 37.

manimekalai:7:40-53.reading: The goddess rises into the sky and leaves; Sudhamathi gets up in burning grief in a city fast asleep, where the drums and lutes of the dancing halls have fallen silent, women who cannot bear their lovers' straying sleep sulking and will not be soothed, and others sleep embracing their lovers on fragrant beds.
manimekalai:7:40-53.nuance: The night catalogue that begins here (to line 86) is one long sentence whose subject is Sudhamathi, awake and alone among sleepers; the sleepers' loves and sulks are the courtesan quarter's life that Madhavi and her daughter have left.
manimekalai:7:40-53.event: The goddess departs into the sky, and Sudhamathi rises in grief in the sleeping city.
manimekalai:7:40-53.unit_note: Starts at line 40, where the narration resumes after the goddess's speech closes at 39; the core unit began at 38, inside her speech.

manimekalai:7:54-69.reading: The sleeping city goes on: small boys worn out with pulling toy carts sleep wearing the five-weapon amulet while their nurses throw mustard against harm and wave incense, the birds of eaves, waters and groves are hushed, the festival's revelry and drums are still; and at midnight come the praises of the palace watch who keep the hours by the water-clock, the long cry of a starving elephant that has broken its restraint in its stall, and the drums of the town watchmen in the streets and lanes.

manimekalai:7:70-84.reading: More night sounds reach Sudhamathi: the drowsy songs of shipwrights drunk on toddy at the harbour, the bathing of women freed from the impurity of childbirth amid smoke of mustard and snake-repelling herbs, the thunderous cry of warriors like tigers at the crossroads of the bhuta offering bali for the victory of the king of the bannered chariot, and the mantra-men who cure new mothers, infants, pregnant women and the wounded calling on the demoness of the common hall to come and take the offering.
manimekalai:7:70-84.nuance: The warriors' cry at 79-80 repeats the Silappathikaram's festival formula for the offering at the bhuta's altar (கொற்றம் கொள்க, உருமுக் குரல்/இடிக் குரல்), here heard as one noise among many in the night. The sense of தீர் வினை மகளிர் (76), women whose task is done or women freed of the birth-pollution, is not certain.

manimekalai:7:85-97.reading: Troubled by all these mingled cries, Sudhamathi leaves the grove in thick darkness by the small gate in the western wall, goes to the Chakravala kottam that the goddess had praised, and sits at one side of the world's hall of charity whose wide gate stands open to all; there, as she is bewildered and afraid, the wondrous image painted on the tall pillar speaks with a divine voice.
manimekalai:7:85-97.nuance: Sudhamathi takes refuge not in a temple of a god but in the open hall of charity of the burning-ground enclosure, where the speaking image is a painting; the help comes from a figure that shows causes (காரணம் காட்டிய, 94).
manimekalai:7:85-97.event: Sudhamathi goes by night to the Chakravala kottam and sits in its hall of charity, where the painted image on the pillar begins to speak.
manimekalai:7:85-97.unit_note: The core unit 85-99 is cut at line 97, where the narration ends with தெய்வக் கிளவியின் and the image's speech begins at 98.

manimekalai:7:98-109.reading: The image addresses Sudhamathi by her former and present births, as the daughter of Ravivarman and queen of Thuchayan of the horse army who, bewildered at Tarai's death, gave up her life before an elephant, and as the daughter of Kausikan of Champai who came to this city with Marutavegan, Virai joined with her elder sister Tarai, now Sudhamathi, and tells her that in seven days at midnight her younger sister, who was Lakshmi, will come knowing both their births, so she should not fear.
manimekalai:7:98-109.nuance: The image is first to reveal that the companions are sisters across births; it names only Sudhamathi's past and leaves Madhavi's (Tarai) implicit, which Manimekalai will supply when she repeats the same address in kaathai 11. Which of the sisters died first and how is told only here in passing, so the story behind 100-101 cannot be fixed from this unit.
manimekalai:7:98-109.event: The pillar image tells Sudhamathi her former birth as Virai and foretells that Manimekalai, once Lakshmi, will come in seven days knowing both their births.
manimekalai:7:98-109.unit_note: Spans the image's whole speech, from its first word at 98 to அஞ்சல்' என்று உரைத்தது at 109; the core units broke at 99 and 115.

manimekalai:7:110-134.reading: Shaken by the words, Sudhamathi waits as the watchmen sleep and the city wakes, conches sounding, elephants and cocks crying, horses and birds rising, flower offerings laid at the gods' altars and the traders' stalls, music and food spread at every door, until the sun rises from the sea; then, aching like a peacock struck by an arrow, she walks through the streets and tells Madhavi everything that happened in the night, and Madhavi, grieving alone that her daughter has not come, sits like a cobra that has lost its gem, like a body that has lost its life.
manimekalai:7:110-134.nuance: The dawn is built of paired lines that repeat a sound with a new sense (பணை நிலைப் புரவி / புள், பூம்பொழில் ஆர்கை / பூங்கொடியார் கை, பண் இயம் / பண்ணியம்), so the whole city's waking is staged as a doubled music against which Madhavi alone does not stir. Madhavi has renounced and been taught that attachment breeds suffering, yet her grief for her child is drawn in the strongest terms of loss. The sense of புலம் புரிச் சங்கம் (114) is not clear.
manimekalai:7:110-134.event: At dawn Sudhamathi tells Madhavi all that happened in the night, and Madhavi sits stricken at her daughter's absence.
manimekalai:7:110-134.unit_note: Starts at line 110, after the image's speech closes at 109, and runs to the kaathai's end; the core boundary at 115/116 fell inside the dawn catalogue, which is one sentence from 110 to 130.

links.note: The couplet says that when the king bends justice the sky withholds rain; the goddess gives the same chain with the planets inserted between sceptre and rain, and aims it at the heir's desire for a nun.
links.teaches: The pair shows the rule's reach being widened: what the Kural ties to judging wrongly the epic applies to a prince's private lust, so the sceptre is bent by desire, not only by a verdict.

gains.a: The goddess's warning is grounded in a known rule of kingship, which shows she argues from ethics shared beyond her own creed rather than from her power.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the wrong is not a judgment and the wrongdoer not yet king, which tests how far its bending of justice extends.

links.note: The Purananuru poem says rice and water are not the world's life, the king is, and he must know it; the goddess says the king's swerving kills life through the failing of rain, so the standing of being the beings' life is lost.
links.teaches: The epic turns the poem's title into a conditional one that a king's own fault cancels, and routes his power over life back through the rain the poem had set below him.

gains.a: Lines 11-12 are read against an old formula of kingship that the goddess is citing in order to take away.
gains.b: The poem's claim that the king, not water, is the world's life gains its limit: in the epic the king governs life only by way of the rain.

links.note: The goddess warns the prince to give up his intent on the ascetic girl; he does not, and is cut down by the vidyadhara Kanchanan as he goes to the girl in her disguise.
links.teaches: The warning threatened failing rain and perishing beings, but the fruit comes as one man's sword on the prince alone, so the cosmic stakes she named collapse into a private death.

links.note: The goddess says only that the cause for the girl's entry into dharma has ripened; at the jewel seat Manimekalai learns that in her birth as Lakshmi a sage foretold that on the day of her trouble the goddess Manimekala would carry her to an island in the south.
links.teaches: The bare 'ripened cause' of this kaathai is revealed later as a prophecy made in a former birth, so the goddess is fulfilling an old word, not deciding afresh.

links.note: Maadalan tells how Kovalan named Madhavi's daughter after the sea goddess who saved his ancestor with the words வந்தேன் அஞ்சல் மணிமேகலை யான்; here the goddess, speaking the same words, adds that on that naming night she told Madhavi in a dream that the child would be a creeper of tapas.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the Manimekalai turning a name given in gratitude for merit of giving into a vocation for renunciation, revealed only now by the goddess herself.

links.note: The goddess's dream foretold a creeper of tapas that would leave Kama helpless; in the Silappathikaram's last kaathai Madhavi gives her daughter to the dharma at the Bodhi seat while Kama throws his bow and arrows on the bare ground.
links.teaches: The earlier epic's closing image of Kama disarmed turns out, read with this dream, to be the fulfilment of a prophecy spoken at the child's naming.

links.note: Both have warriors at the bhuta's altar in Puhar crying that the victorious king take victory (கொற்றம் கொள்க) with a thunder voice as they offer bali; the Silappathikaram stages it as the festival's central rite, the Manimekalai lists it among the night noises a grieving woman hears.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the same offering formula moves from the heart of a royal festival to one sound among drunk shipwrights and mantra-men, which shows how the later epic pushes the blood rite to the margin of its story.

links.note: The painted image on the pillar of the hall speaks at night to frightened Sudhamathi; later the same image speaks to Kanchanan just after he has killed the prince, telling him the woman he sought was Manimekalai in disguise.
links.teaches: The pillar's voice comes once in time, to comfort with knowledge of past births, and once too late, to tell a killer what he did not know, so the same speaking image marks both the gift and the failure of right knowing.

links.note: The image addresses Sudhamathi with இரவிவன்மன் ஒரு பெரு மகளே, துரகத் தானைத் துச்சயன் தேவி and promises that Lakshmi will come knowing both births; returned from the island, Manimekalai addresses her mothers with the same lines and names them Tarai and Virai.
links.teaches: The prophecy is fulfilled in the very words of the image, now in the girl's mouth, and the later scene supplies what the image left out: Madhavi too was a sister, Tarai.

links.note: Madhavi tells how the teacher Aravanar taught her that suffering comes of attachment and freedom from it of letting go; here, a renouncer, she sits like a body without life because her daughter has not come.
links.teaches: The pair shows the epic letting its own renouncer fall short of the teaching she received, so taking robes does not by itself end attachment to a child.

new_concepts.gloss: a cause or condition that ripens and brings an event about; the Manimekalai's ஏது நிகழ்ச்சி
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (lines 20, 29: ஏது முதிர்ந்தது, ஏதுப் பல உள)

new_concepts.gloss: the offering of blood or food laid before a fierce deity as a due owed to her
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (lines 80, 85: இடும் பலி, எறி பலி); id as declared in silappathikaram ch017

source_issues: The core unit boundaries at 24/25, 37/38, 99/100 and 115/116 fall inside sentences or speeches; the units are re-cut at 14, 25, 39, 97 and 109.

Lines 117-124 are paired lines that repeat a sound with a different sense (ஆர்கைப் / ஆர் கைப், பண் இயம் / பண்ணியம்); the word division of 119-120 in this text decides the pun and may differ in other editions.
Line 134 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle, so the last sentence reads as cut short in this text.
Line 114 புலம் புரிச் சங்கம் is obscure: the conch of the learned, or a play on வலம்புரிச் சங்கம் in 113.
